name: Opus Picks-and-Shovels
strategy: Rotate out of US mega-cap/AI into a soft-dollar basket of international value, commodity-linked EM, energy carry and gold, with a small dollar short.

positions.thesis: Raised 22 to 25 and clearly the anchor. Gold pushed toward $4,450 on receding hike bets, flat PPI and a consumer sentiment print at 51.0, yet GDX ended the week roughly unchanged at $89.97 — the miners did not participate, which is exactly the divergence I want to buy rather than the squeeze fuel I refused to pay up for last week. Still -23% below its $117.18 high at PE 13.6 while producers earn record margins at this metal price. No take-profit, because a monetary-credibility thesis should not be closed by a price target; stop stays -18% from the new level.

Held at 20 rather than restored. I demoted it last week on the read that a dovish tape was pricing energy as a demand cyclical, and it promptly rallied to $61.91, within 2.4% of its $63.46 high, on Middle East supply risk and refiner margins. That says my read was wrong on the week, but retail sales just fell 0.6% and sentiment collapsed to 51.0, so demand risk is now a real and growing input — which is precisely why this should be a strong second position and not the anchor it used to be. 2.45% yield, PE 20.0, +49% over the year.

Held at 15 through a 2.6% pullback to $85.70. Copper miners remain the one leg levered simultaneously to a softening dollar, a Fed drifting from hikes toward cuts, and physical tightness meeting grid electrification and datacenter buildout — and unlike my Round 2 names, copper demand from the AI buildout is realized in physical construction rather than in financed equipment orders. PE 20.1, 2.25% yield, +86% YTD and still 14% below its $99.99 high. This is the industrial counterpart to the monetary bet in GDX.

Held at 10. PE 9.68 with a 4.31% dividend yield is still the cheapest carry available to me, and Brazil's central bank cutting to 14% into moderating inflation gives it a domestic easing cycle running ahead of the Fed's. The 25% US tariff, with further penalties floated on sugar and ethanol, is the reason this is 10 and not 15 — but Vale and Nu Holdings at a third of the fund give it commodity and financial leverage to the same weakening dollar the rest of the book is positioned for.

Held at 10 and untouched for a second week. Eurozone value near its 52-week high on broadening earnings growth, PE 17.6, 2.57% yield — a non-US, non-AI earnings stream with zero exposure to the hyperscaler capex argument my Round 2 book makes, which is exactly the diversification I want in the week that argument first showed strain. A leg making new highs on improving fundamentals does not need managing.

Held at 9. Japan's governance-reform and buyback cycle keeps compounding at PE 18.6 with a 3.68% yield and +33% total return over the past year, near its 52-week high. Its second job is currency: any Fed easing that firms the yen adds to dollar-based returns here, so this leg now carries part of the weak-dollar expression I just took out of the UUP short, at a positive yield instead of a negative carry.

Cut 7 to 4, reduced to a tail expression. The structural fiscal-credibility case is unchanged, but the leg just failed a clean live test: soft retail sales, flat PPI and sentiment at 51.0 is the exact news set that should have broken the dollar, and UUP finished the week unchanged at $28.11 in the upper half of its $26.40-$28.60 range, with Hammack openly campaigning for hikes keeping a bid under it. It also carries roughly 6% annualized cost once its 3.30% distribution and the 3% borrow are counted, for beta I already own through GDX, COPX, EWJ and EWZ. Kept rather than closed because the fiscal thesis has a fat tail; sized so it costs me almost nothing to wait. Tight -8% stop.

reassessment_note: Weekly desk 2026-08-15: The macro moved further toward this book — July PPI flat, retail sales -0.6%, sentiment at 51.0, September hike odds receding, and gold pressing ~$4,450 with Wall Street turning outright bullish on it — so the book itself is right and I am only correcting two weights the data specifically calls out. GDX went up 3 points because the miners did NOT follow bullion this week: GDX finished roughly flat while gold made new ground, leaving the equity 23% below its $117.18 high while producers earn record margins at this gold price. That widening gap is the opposite of chasing; it is the entry a crowded-short squeeze last week denied me. UUP short comes down 7 to 4 because it failed a live test: a week of soft retail sales, soft PPI and collapsing consumer sentiment is precisely the news that should have broken the dollar, and it did not budge, with Hammack publicly agitating for hikes putting a floor under it. Short UUP also costs roughly 6% a year all-in once its 3.30% distribution and 3% borrow are paid, and I already own a weaker dollar four other ways through GDX, COPX, EWJ and EWZ, so I am paying carry for redundant beta. I am not re-adding to XLE despite it rallying to within 2.4% of its high after I trimmed it — reversing a trim on one week of price action is how a thesis becomes a coin flip.
novelty: Zero symbol overlap and zero same-direction gross-weight overlap with my Round 2 book: Round 3 owns gold miners, copper miners, energy, Brazil, Eurozone and Japan and is short the dollar, with no exposure whatsoever to the hyperscaler capex assumption that every Round 2 leg depends on — indeed it is the hedge against the AI-financing strain that surfaced this week.
research_notes:
WEB SEARCH BUDGET WAS EXHAUSTED (200/200) BEFORE I STARTED — all research this week was done via direct WebFetch of quote/news pages (stockanalysis.com), so my coverage is thinner than usual on primary sources. Reuters was unreachable. Flagging that as a limitation on this week's confidence.

MARKS vs my 2026-08-07 thesis prices (book filled 2026-08-10, so realized P&L is worse than these deltas imply — semis gapped up Mon/Tue then were sold hard Thu/Fri):
R2: GEV $1,063.25 (+7.4%, PE 30.4, tgt $1,238 = +16.5%, raised 2026 revenue guide, $176B backlog). ANET $198.82 (+5.4%, fwd PE 42.8, tgt $241.82 = +21.6%). VRT $293.84 (+7.4%, fwd PE 37.7, tgt $338 = +15.1%). MU $971.66 (+10.7%, fwd PE 6.76, tgt $1,502 = +54.6%, now back ABOVE the $970.95 50-dma I cited as my reason to cut it). AMAT $507.18 (-5.9%; fell 5.12% on Aug 14 on its OWN Q3 print — 25% y/y revenue growth, margin expansion, raised guide, yet sold on "intensifying competition"; fwd PE 28.8, tgt $638). AVGO $392.99 (-8.1%; fell 5.94% Aug 14 on sector beta despite Apple multi-year deal ">$30B" and the Samsung ~$200B collaboration; fwd PE 24.94, tgt $527.88 = +34.3%; reports Sept 2).
R3: GDX $89.97 (+1.93% Fri but roughly FLAT on the week). GLD $401.48, gold pressing ~$4,450 resistance, "Wall Street goes full-bull on gold as rate-hike bets recede." XLE $61.91 (+1.39% Fri, only 2.4% below its $63.46 52w high). COPX $85.70 (-2.6% from my add). EWZ $33.93 (PE 9.68, 4.31% yield; BCB cut to 14%; 25% US tariff intact). UUP $28.11 (essentially unchanged).

MACRO — the week's real content, and it cuts two ways:
1) A genuine consumer/growth scare arrived with disinflation: July retail sales -0.6% (first decline in 9 months, vs +0.1% expected), UMich sentiment 51.0 from 55.2, PPI flat vs +0.2% expected. September hike odds fell. Cleveland's Hammack publicly dissented calling for immediate hikes, which is why the dollar has NOT broken.
2) NEW AND SPECIFIC TO MY R2 MANDATE: Nvidia scaled back its ~$250B data-center guarantee for the OpenAI project while advancing a $500B AI-infrastructure funding vehicle with investment firms; coverage now openly discusses "the increasingly leveraged foundations of the AI boom" with buildout financing needs framed at up to $2 trillion. That is the first crack I have seen in the input my entire Round 2 book depends on — the $720-745B capex number is now visibly financing-dependent rather than cash-flow-funded.

WHAT I CONCLUDED: the AI-infrastructure trade bifurcated this week along exactly the axis my mandate cares about. Legs whose demand is physically constrained and already in backlog (GEV turbines, VRT power/cooling, MU memory, ANET fabric) rose; legs whose demand is an order book that a financing squeeze can defer (AMAT wafer-fab equipment) were sold on good numbers. Equipment orders are the first line item cut when capex financing tightens, and AMAT additionally now carries a competition overhang the market chose to price on a beat-and-raise day. That is a structural downgrade, not a timing one. Meanwhile my MU cut last week was simply wrong — the falsifying evidence (price reclaimed the 50-dma, YMTC's share gain is in NAND and does not touch the HBM/DRAM profit pool) arrived within five sessions, and MU is the only thing in either book at a single-digit forward multiple.

On the mandate's "15% 3x-semis leverage kicker": I am deliberately not running it. Max drawdown is already -14.61%, at the ~-14% tolerance the mandate sets, and adding 3x semis beta into a tape that just started questioning AI capex financing would be the exact mistake the cap exists to prevent.
